business: Rich's Plumbing Heating & Air Conditioning, Inc.

opportunities.title: 24/7 intake and emergency-triage voice agent on the single main line, with web-form instant response
opportunities.problem: Every sales and contact path funnels to one phone number, (732) 257-1663, published identically for the East Brunswick, Elizabeth and Bayville offices; the site offers no scheduler, chat or self-serve slot picker, so a small office staff is the only way a customer can book. The company simultaneously advertises 24/7 emergency service with a stated 60-minute response time, which means that same small staff (or an answering service) must absorb after-hours volume and manually run safety triage questions - where the leak is, whether water is still flowing, whether the shutoff was closed, whether there is electrical hazard - before anyone can decide to roll a truck.
evidence: Single phone number published for all three office addresses, and pages tell callers they will reach 'our friendly, knowledgeable office staff' - one centralized intake point, no per-location lines (https://www.richsplumbing.com/contact-us/)

Lead capture is a two-step form (phone + name, then address, comments, optional SMS consent) posting to /api/lead with no calendar or time-slot picker; the emergency page says online scheduling is 'available for service requests' but directs active emergencies to call, so the web path is a callback request, not real-time dispatch (https://www.richsplumbing.com/plumbing/emergency-plumbing/)
24/7 emergency service advertised site-wide with a 60-minute emergency response claim (qualified by conditions and location) (https://www.richsplumbing.com/plumbing/emergency-plumbing/)

Pre-call triage is explicitly manual: staff are expected to establish where the leak/backup is, whether water is still flowing, whether the shutoff was closed and whether electrical hazards exist (https://www.richsplumbing.com/plumbing/emergency-plumbing/)
No live chat, SMS chatbot or online scheduler detected on any page reviewed; contact paths are phone plus form only (https://www.richsplumbing.com/contact-us/)
Office staff currently make outbound 'tech is on the way' calls as a manual courtesy that customers praise - proof the comms workflow is staff-driven and high-touch (https://www.richsplumbing.com/)

Cost benchmark: NJ annual median wage $47,740 for Customer Service Representatives (43-4051) and $54,590 for Dispatchers (43-5032), May 2025 OEWS (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000043405113 and https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000043503213)

Throughput benchmark (label check: this is an NBER working paper, 31161, later published in QJE 2025 vol 140(2), so the peer-reviewed version is the journal article, not the URL cited): generative-AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour 14% on average across 5,179 support agents, 34% for novices (https://www.nber.org/papers/w31161)
opportunities.agent_design: Voice agent answers the main line after 2-3 rings during peak overflow and on first ring after hours and on weekends, for all three locations. It runs a fixed safety-triage script (water still flowing, shutoff closed, electrical hazard present, sewage backup, gas smell / no heat in freezing weather), classifies the call as true emergency vs same-day vs routine, captures address, access notes, equipment type and age, and either books a slot against technician availability or takes a callback with a promised window. It sends SMS confirmation and a 'tech en route' notification, and writes the record through the existing /api/lead endpoint plus a side store so nothing is lost. Hard human-approval boundaries: the agent never quotes a price, never commits to a gas or electrical safety diagnosis, and any emergency flagged as hazardous is warm-transferred to the on-call technician's mobile rather than handled to completion. Staff review a daily exception queue of low-confidence classifications. The web form agent replies within roughly a minute with two or three slot options and a Synchrony financing link for replacement-type inquiries.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: A chatbot subscription cannot answer a telephone. This needs SIP/telephony integration with the published number, after-hours routing and warm transfer to an on-call rotation, a scheduling calendar or dispatch system it can write to, SMS with the TCPA consent the site already collects on its form, sub-second latency so callers do not hang up, and fail-safe behaviour that never strands a burst-pipe call. Getting the emergency escalation wrong is a reputational and possibly safety event, and the site's under-represented-negative review pattern means a bad after-hours experience lands publicly on Google.

impact_estimate.range: $20,000-$50,000 per year in avoided intake labor plus recovered after-hours and overflow bookings
impact_estimate.assumptions: Labor component: intake/dispatch handling is assumed to consume roughly 2.0-3.5 FTE-equivalents today (inference: three locations on one number, 624 geotagged jobs in the review map, plus 24/7 coverage) and the agent realistically offsets 0.35-0.8 FTE of overflow and after-hours answering, valued at the NJ CSR ($47,740) to dispatcher ($54,590) medians. I deliberately do not transfer the working paper's +14%-per-agent figure directly, because that study measures support-issue throughput by trained staff, not emergency dispatch, so only a fraction is assumed. Revenue component: assumes 10-30 after-hours or missed calls per month convert, and a $250-$600 average job value - inference from published coupons ($189 tune-up, $75 drain clearing, $50 off a plumbing repair, $500 off a boiler install), not a published ticket average. Excluded: any change in average ticket from better triage, and any 60-minute-response compliance gain.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 2-4 weeks on the single published number, after-hours and overflow only: triage script covering the site's own four safety questions, emergency/hazard warm-transfer path to on-call, SMS confirmation, booking or callback capture, and a call log with transcripts. Deliverables are a containment report (calls fully handled vs escalated), escalation accuracy audited against staff review of the same calls, and a booked-after-hours count. No change to the existing phone menu or dispatch software during the pilot, and daytime in-hours calls stay with staff.

opportunities.title: Unsold-estimate follow-up and coupon/financing nudge agent
opportunities.problem: Estimates are produced on site and explained verbally, and that conversation appears to be the only conversion attempt: there is no published price list, no online quote, no visible e-signature and no evidence of a CRM to track an estimate that was declined or 'let me think about it'. Reviews describe pricing as fair but 'not cheap' or 'a little high', which is exactly the objection that needs a second, structured touch (financing, a published coupon, a service-plan comparison) days later. Separately, six coupons are redeemed through manual codes and URL parameters (RICH50, TUNE189, WATER50, BOILER500, DRAIN75, HVAC300), so whether a homeowner actually gets the discount depends on staff catching it on the call.
evidence: Estimates for most services are done on site and then discussed with the homeowner, with no published price list or quote calculator anywhere on the site (https://www.richsplumbing.com/plumbing/emergency-plumbing/)
Six online coupons claimed via URL parameter and manual codes, a trackable but staff-dependent redemption path (https://www.richsplumbing.com/)

Consumer financing via Synchrony is embedded in the header, product pages and a financing page - the financing offer exists but reaching the right declined-estimate customer is a manual step (https://www.richsplumbing.com/contact-us/)

Review theme: pricing is described as fair but 'not cheap' / 'a little high' by some reviewers, with transparency credited to on-site explanation of costs, implying objection handling happens once, verbally, in person (https://www.richsplumbing.com/reviews/)
No e-signature, estimate-follow-up (SMS/email sequence) or online scheduler detected on any page reviewed; contact paths are phone plus form only (https://www.richsplumbing.com/contact-us/)
Repeat and long-tenure customers are common in reviews, so a booked-but-declined estimate is a relationship that can be reopened rather than a lost stranger (https://www.richsplumbing.com/reviews/)

Lifecycle role whose work this absorbs is the NJ customer-service/booking seat: annual medians $47,740 (CSR 43-4051) and $54,590 (Dispatchers 43-5032), May 2025 OEWS (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000043405113)
opportunities.agent_design: Triggered when a technician or office staffer closes an estimate as declined, deferred or pending. The agent takes the structured estimate (line items, options, expiry), the customer's stated objection and the visit transcript, then drafts a short sequence: same-day recap with the numbers and a financing link, a day-3 answer to the specific objection (price vs repair-vs-replace math, available coupon such as the $500 boiler or $300 HVAC discount, or maintenance-plan entitlement), a day-10 expiry reminder, and a day-21 close. Replies are classified (ready to book, question, cheaper alternative, hard no) and ready-to-book replies create a callback task on the office calendar; nothing is auto-booked without staff confirmation. Every message is drafted, queued and approved by office staff during the pilot; auto-send only after accuracy review. The agent also reads the coupon code into the job record so the discount is applied without the customer having to mention it.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: This is not a marketing blast: it requires an estimate data model, per-customer objection state, consent-aware SMS/email, intent classification on inbound replies, and writes into whatever the office uses as a system of record, plus a financing deep link. A generic AI writing tool cannot know which estimate is still open, cannot stop itself from re-contacting someone who already booked, and cannot hand a hot reply back to the calendar.

impact_estimate.range: $6,000-$28,000 per year in gross profit from re-opened estimates
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference, not measured: the company publishes no estimate count, close rate or average ticket. Assumes 40-120 estimates per month at three locations, a 2-5% incremental recovery on stalled ones (2-6 extra jobs per month), and a $400-$1,200 average job value inferred from the coupon ladder ($50 off a repair, $75 drain clearing, $189 tune-up, $300 HVAC and $500 boiler discounts implying high-hundreds to four-figure jobs). Gross margin assumed 30-40% on service work. No labor savings claimed, because the sequence replaces a courtesy call that may not currently happen at all. Sensitivity: at 1 extra job per month the benefit is roughly $1.5k-$6k per year, below the cost of the build, which is why the pilot must measure stall volume in week one before committing.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 3 weeks over the prior 60 days of declined or pending estimates: reconcile how many stalled estimates actually exist and in what form (paper, spreadsheet, software), then run the agent as a draft-and-approve assistant. Deliverable is a measured reply rate and re-book count against a defined baseline, plus a written loop on which objection phrasing converts.

opportunities.title: Maintenance-plan records and renewal knowledge agent for office staff and technicians
opportunities.problem: The paid maintenance plan is sold partly on the promise that the company keeps 'all records' - equipment, serial numbers, prior technicians, warranty dates and service history - and gives plan members top-priority scheduling. That recordkeeping is currently presented as a manual service benefit, and there is no visible CRM or customer portal, so the knowledge sits in whatever the office staff person remembers or can find. Every plan renewal, seasonal tune-up reminder and warranty question depends on someone manually reading paper or spreadsheets, which caps how many plans the same small office team can carry as the company expands to Bayville and Toms River.
evidence: Maintenance plan markets seasonal check-ups, priority regular and emergency scheduling, discounts, and 'record-keeping of equipment serial numbers and service history' as a service the company performs by hand (https://www.richsplumbing.com/hvac-services/maintenance-plan/)
No CRM, dispatch platform or customer portal is visible anywhere on the public site; the only backend path detected is a form posting to /api/lead (https://www.richsplumbing.com/contact-us/)

Review evidence shows long-tenure, repeat customers ('customers for 20 years', third-time callers), meaning equipment histories and warranty windows are deep and long-lived, not one-off (https://www.richsplumbing.com/reviews/)

Technicians are described as 10-15 years trained and reviews are tech-specific by name, so service history is attached to individual techs who may leave - a tacit knowledge risk (https://www.richsplumbing.com/about-us/)

One small office staff appears to carry intake, scheduling, estimates and follow-up across three locations, so plan administration competes with same-day phone volume (https://www.richsplumbing.com/about-us/)

Cost benchmark for the administrative seat that absorbs this work: NJ dispatcher median $54,590 and CSR median $47,740, May 2025 OEWS (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/OEUS340000000000043503213)

Label check on the closest automation analogue: the arXiv technician-routing paper (2211.16968) is a preprint, not peer-reviewed; it reports roughly 16% travel-time reduction on one telecom company's instance and does not study residential plumbing/HVAC, so I cite it only as directional support for scheduling work, not for this opportunity's numbers (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.16968)
opportunities.agent_design: First a small structured build (capability D inside this opportunity): a plan-customer record store with property, equipment make/model/serial, install date, warranty end date, refrigerant-relevant notes, prior jobs and the assigned technician, populated by extracting from existing paper, PDFs and spreadsheets with human verification of every field on a sample. On top of it, a knowledge agent that staff and techs query in plain language - 'what's the serial and warranty end date on the Smith boiler', 'what did we quote this customer last spring', 'which plan customers are due a heating tune-up in the next 45 days' - with every answer citing the underlying record. It generates seasonal reminder lists, renewal notices and a pre-visit briefing for the tech, and posts the technician's end-of-job notes back to the record with the tech's approval. Human approval gates: any customer-facing message is drafted and approved by office staff; warranty-claim or refrigerant-log entries are always technician-authored and technician-signed, never agent-generated, given Section 608 recordkeeping exposure.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: The hard part is not the conversation, it is the data: decades of serial numbers, model numbers, warranty windows and job notes in inconsistent formats, which must be normalized, deduplicated by property and equipment, and kept auditable because the same records feed warranty claims and refrigerant/OSHA obligations. Retrieval must cite the exact record so a staffer can defend a warranty position, and the agent must write back into job history, which no off-the-shelf chatbot does. This also touches homeowner addresses and payment history, so it needs tightly scoped or private deployment rather than a consumer-grade assistant.

impact_estimate.range: $6,000-$22,000 per year (mostly staff hours recovered, plus a modest renewal-retention effect)
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference only; plan price, member count and current churn are not published. Labor: 3-6 hours per week of lookup, reminder list building and renewal admin at the NJ dispatcher median ($54,590/yr, roughly $26/hr base, more fully loaded) gives $4k-$8k. Retention: assumes 200-600 plan members (inference from 624 geotagged jobs in the review map and a 12+ town service area) and 3-8% fewer lapsed renewals, worth $2k-$14k depending on an assumed $150-$350 annual plan price - the widest assumption in this brief. Excludes revenue from tune-ups that convert to repairs. If member count turns out to be under 150, this opportunity should be reframed as pure staff-efficiency and may not clear a build cost.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 3 weeks: digitize and verify equipment records for 150-250 plan customers, stand up the staff/tech Q&A agent with record-level citations, run one seasonal reminder campaign from agent-generated lists, and audit 30 records field-by-field for accuracy. Deliverable is a measured lookup time before vs after, an accuracy score, and a count of plan customers whose warranty or service history was previously unfindable.

lead_score.rationale: Pain (24/30): unusually concrete, site-verified operational signals for a business this size - one phone number across three offices, no scheduler or chat anywhere, an advertised 60-minute emergency response that depends on manual triage questions, and maintenance-plan recordkeeping marketed as a hand-performed service. It is docked because these are inferences from the public site, not confirmed process, and the review base is company-curated through a RealWorkLabs widget, so the negative side is under-represented. Fit (19/20): opportunities A, C and D apply directly with no hardware and no consumer chatbot exposure; the modern Astro site with a JSON /api/lead endpoint gives a clean integration seam. Ability to pay (11/20): three leased offices, Synchrony consumer financing, a paid maintenance plan and roughly daily content production all indicate real revenue and investment appetite, but headcount, revenue and fleet are unpublished, it is family-owned and price-sensitive per its own reviews, and no owner or GM name is public, so qualification is unproven. Ease (11/15): the sell is easy to frame (they already promise 24/7 and speed) and the web layer is modern, but the phone system, call volume, dispatch software and current missed-call rate are all unknown, and a 24/7 emergency scope raises the reliability bar for a first engagement. Strategic (14/15): the pattern - one number, no booking engine, manual plan records, SEO-heavy lead generation - repeats across nearly every NJ plumbing/HVAC contractor, so the assets built here (triage script, estimate follow-up, plan record store) are reusable across the vertical. Residual gaps that keep this out of the high 80s: no named decision maker, no verified employee count or revenue, and no first-hand confirmation of what software, if any, runs the office.

best_evidence_signal: One phone number, (732) 257-1663, is published for all three offices and every page funnels to it, with no scheduler, chat or slot picker on the site - while the company advertises 24/7 emergency service and a 60-minute response target (https://www.richsplumbing.com/contact-us/)
